fit.text: Command-line programs and applications assembled from Go packages; the example needs no external module.

prerequisites.text: Use a text editor and terminal. Learn package main, imports and the main entry function.

execution.text: The go command builds and runs source; go run hello.go is the direct path for this single-file example.

behavior.text: Object lifetimes are managed through garbage collection; allocation patterns still affect runtime overhead.

fit.text: Gosu provides typed JVM programs with Java-library interoperability, properties, closures and extension methods.

prerequisites.text: The checked GosuLab quickstart uses JDK 1.8 and JAVA_HOME. Verify the chosen distribution's JDK requirements before installation.

execution.text: A .gsp program contains executable statements; gosu hello.gsp runs it without a Java-style main wrapper.

behavior.text: Variable types can be inferred; properties and enhancements extend the Java-style object model.

tooling.text: GosuLab offers an editor and example execution; documented program classpaths can include directories, jars or Maven coordinates.

maintenance.text: Record the JDK and dependencies used. The documentation notes that the IntelliJ plugin can lag newer language features.

costs.text: The checked Gosu source uses Apache-2.0 terms; the JDK and Maven-resolved libraries carry separate licenses.

example.run_instructions: Install and configure the selected Gosu distribution as its quickstart describes, then run gosu hello.gsp from a terminal with Gosu available on PATH.

fit.text: Groovy supports JVM scripting, domain-specific languages and Java-library integration; object-oriented and functional styles can coexist.

prerequisites.text: The checked Groovy 6.0 installation guide requires Java 17 or later. Configure JAVA_HOME and the selected Groovy distribution's bin directory.

execution.text: groovy runs a source script by compiling and executing it; applications can also embed Groovy through JVM dependencies.

behavior.text: The language supports dynamic and static typing, closures and static compilation; select the required checking mode deliberately.

tooling.text: groovysh provides an interactive shell and groovyConsole a graphical console; the CLI accepts scripts and expressions.

maintenance.text: Keep Groovy, the JDK and build dependencies compatible; installation prerequisites vary by Groovy release.

costs.text: Apache Groovy's primary grant is Apache-2.0; the LICENSE file also records included third-party terms.

example.run_instructions: With the selected Groovy distribution and a compatible JDK configured, run groovy hello.groovy.

implementation.name: HashiCorp HCL 2 parser library
implementation.version_scope: The HCL syntax/parser library, not a Terraform or other host-product license.

sources.label: HCL library architecture and host-defined schemas
HCL library license

fit.text: Human-oriented configuration for developer tools and services; the consuming application defines its schema.

prerequisites.text: Learn attributes, blocks and expressions, then the particular host application's accepted names and values.

execution.text: A host loads HCL and interprets its content. Parsing a file does not deploy infrastructure by itself.

behavior.text: Native HCL and JSON forms share a model; available variables and functions are provided by the host.

tooling.text: HCL 2 supplies Go libraries for parsing and evaluation, with Go modules required for integration.

maintenance.text: HCL 2's Go API is incompatible with HCL 1; coordinate parser and host migrations.

costs.text: The HCL parser's terms do not establish the license or price of a product consuming HCL.

example.run_instructions: Parse service.hcl using an HCL 2 host that defines a service block with one label and a port attribute. This is illustrative configuration, not a standalone deployment command.
example.expected_result: The parser can represent the web service block and numeric port. A host schema must validate and interpret it; no service is launched.

licenses.scope: HashiCorp HCL library covered by its repository license.
licenses.notice: Host tools and their modules need separate license checks.

implementation.name: Microsoft DirectX Shader Compiler (DXC)
implementation.version_scope: DXC shader-model-6 pixel-shader workflow using the documented CLI; compiler, graphics API, driver and shader model are separate version choices.

sources.label: Microsoft Learn: HLSL and programmable shader stages
Microsoft Learn: shader input/output semantics
Microsoft DXC: compiler outputs and execution requirements
Microsoft DXC: entry-point, target-profile and output flags
Microsoft DXC: University of Illinois/NCSA and component notices

fit.text: Write GPU graphics or compute shader stages used by a host application. The shader is one part of a graphics or compute pipeline, not a standalone desktop application.

prerequisites.text: Learn shader stages, vector types and input/output semantics. Install DXC for compilation; executing its DXIL output additionally needs a compatible host API and graphics-driver environment.

execution.text: DXC selects the entry point with -E and shader profile with -T, then writes a compiled object through -Fo. A host application loads and invokes the shader.

behavior.text: HLSL has C-like shader syntax. System-value semantics connect values to pipeline stages; SV_Target supplies a pixel shader's render-target output.

tooling.text: Use dxc for compilation and its help output for flags. DXC also exposes a compiler DLL interface and shader debug/reflection information.

maintenance.text: Record the compiler version and target profile with shader artifacts. Driver/runtime support and the host's pipeline bindings must match the compiled shader.

costs.text: Plan for the host application and graphics environment as well as shader tooling. DXC's own grant and its bundled component notices need separate review.

example.run_instructions: With DXC installed, save hello.hlsl and run dxc -E main -T ps_6_0 -Fo hello.dxil hello.hlsl. This compiles a pixel shader; displaying a result requires a host graphics application that binds it to a render pipeline.
example.expected_result: Produces hello.dxil containing a compiled pixel shader. When invoked in a correctly configured rendering pipeline, its output is the constant RGBA vector (1, 0, 0, 1); the compilation command does not display an image.

licenses.component: DirectX Shader Compiler's own covered source
licenses.scope: The University of Illinois/NCSA grant identified by the DXC README and license file; third-party parts have additional notices.
licenses.notice: Preserve source/binary notices and review the complete LICENSE.TXT and distribution notices rather than treating every bundled component as NCSA.

fit.text: Typed application and web-server code using HHVM. The runtime executes Hack programs; server deployment also needs the chosen web-server configuration.

prerequisites.text: Install HHVM and the Hack tools, learn function/type syntax, and use a .hack file with an __EntryPoint function. Project typechecking requires its documented setup.

execution.text: Run hh_client to check the configured project, then use hhvm hello.hack for command-line execution. Typechecking and execution are separate steps.

behavior.text: Hack has a static type system with subtyping, nullable types, inference and refinement. EntryPoint identifies the startup function independently of its name.

tooling.text: Use hh_client for type errors and IDE information, HHVM for running code, and the Hack Standard Library where required by the application.

maintenance.text: Keep file includes/autoloading and project typechecker configuration consistent. Web-server execution is a different deployment workflow from a standalone .hack file.

costs.text: Plan for the HHVM host and application dependencies. The MIT typechecker/library grants do not replace the runtime's PHP and Zend notices.

example.run_instructions: Save hello.hack and run hhvm hello.hack with HHVM installed. For project analysis, configure the project as described in the getting-started guide and run hh_client from its directory.
example.expected_result: Prints PLLDN followed by a newline.

implementation.name: Hare macOS port (hshq/harelang)
implementation.version_scope: The independently maintained macOS port named by the upstream FAQ. Licensing below applies to this inspected port's build driver and standard-library source, not an inferred current SourceHut grant.

sources.label: Hare: language scope, static types and manual memory management
Hare tutorial: startup function, error assertion and compile/run workflow
Hare upstream FAQ: independent macOS port and support boundary
hshq Hare macOS port: components and licensing
hshq Hare port: Darwin build setup
hshq Hare build driver: CLI commands and GPL-3.0-only identifier
hshq Hare standard library: MPL-2.0 text

fit.text: Systems programs with static types, explicit memory management and a small runtime. This selected implementation is a macOS port, whose support is separate from upstream Hare.

prerequisites.text: Learn types, namespaces and explicit error handling. For this macOS port, follow README.darwin and install the required harec/compiler backend and platform build tools.

execution.text: The hare build driver compiles and runs source through its run subcommand; build creates an executable and test runs embedded tests.

behavior.text: Memory management is explicit. The starter's ! asserts that printing succeeds and aborts on a reported error; larger programs should handle or propagate errors deliberately.

tooling.text: The inspected port provides build, run, test, deps and version CLI commands. Its build setup separately selects harec, qbe, assembler and linker tools.

maintenance.text: Pin the port and toolchain revision. Upstream's tutorial targets a stable Hare release and can differ from master; upstream explicitly separates support for this macOS port.

costs.text: Account for the port's build environment and dependencies. Its GPL build-driver source and MPL standard-library source have distinct redistribution terms.

example.run_instructions: After installing a working version of the hshq macOS port and its required toolchain, save hello.ha and run hare run hello.ha. The shared Hare tutorial also documents hare build -o hello hello.ha followed by ./hello. Check the port's compiler/library version if tutorial syntax differs.
example.expected_result: Prints PLLDN followed by a newline when the port's compiler and library accept this starter. A printing error trips the explicit ! assertion.

licenses.scope: The build-driver source in this inspected port; cmd/hare/main.ha declares GPL-3.0-only.
licenses.notice: Review GPL obligations for redistribution or modification of covered tools. The separate harec compiler and backend require their own component review.

licenses.scope: The standard-library source in this inspected port, whose COPYING contains MPL version 2.0.
licenses.notice: Review the MPL terms and file-specific notices for covered modifications and redistribution; this is not a license assigned to every Hare application.

implementation.name: Glasgow Haskell Compiler (GHC)
implementation.version_scope: GHC 9.14.1 user-guide workflows; starter uses a Haskell 2010-compatible subset and no external packages.

GHC 9.14.1 introduction and compiler license
GHC 9.14.1: running source with runghc
GHCup: compilation, interpreter, signatures and project tools
GHC's own three-clause BSD license grant

fit.text: General-purpose functional programs built from expressions, typed modules and reusable functions. The language specification leaves the concrete compilation environment to implementations such as GHC.

prerequisites.text: Install a GHC toolchain and learn expressions, type signatures, pattern matching and the IO distinction. Begin with runghc or GHCi before adding a package build.

execution.text: GHC offers batch compilation and GHCi; runghc interprets a source file without a separate compile-and-run step.

behavior.text: Haskell 2010 specifies pure functions, non-strict semantics, static polymorphic types and monadic I/O. GHC adds optional language extensions beyond that baseline.

tooling.text: Use GHCi to inspect types, GHC warnings for source checks, and Cabal or Stack for projects with modules and external packages.

maintenance.text: Record compiler and package choices, declared language/extensions and dependencies in the project. GHC's introduction notes that some toolchain updates require recompilation of dependent code.

costs.text: Plan for build tools, package dependencies and deployment libraries. GHC's own BSD grant does not establish the licenses of every external package.

example.run_instructions: Save hello.hs and run runghc hello.hs with GHC installed. Alternatively, compile with ghc hello.hs and run the produced platform-specific executable.
example.expected_result: Prints PLLDN followed by a newline.

licenses.scope: The GHC compiler grant reproduced in its license and user guide; separately supplied libraries and platform tools require their own review.
licenses.notice: Preserve required source/binary notices and observe endorsement restrictions for covered distribution.

Haxe manual: first program and interpreter command
Haxe language introduction: JavaScript, JVM and interpreter workflows

fit.text: Cross-platform application code with classes and a shared language; each compilation target still has its own APIs and deployment environment.

prerequisites.text: Install the Haxe compiler, learn class and function syntax, and match a class's name to its .hx filename. The interpreter starter needs no separate target runtime.

execution.text: Haxe can execute the program with --interp or compile it to a chosen target such as JavaScript or JVM bytecode.

behavior.text: The language combines a type system with object-oriented constructs. A common source language does not make all target libraries or runtime behavior interchangeable.

tooling.text: The command-line compiler selects a main class and a target. Start with --interp before adding JavaScript, JVM or another target toolchain.

maintenance.text: Choose and test the target environment deliberately; emitted JavaScript and JVM output need their respective hosts, unlike the compiler's interpreter workflow.

costs.text: Budget for the selected target's tools and deployment. The compiler and standard library use different licenses; review shipped dependencies separately.

example.run_instructions: Save as Main.hx in a working directory with Haxe installed, then run haxe -main Main --interp. A separate target runtime is unnecessary for this interpreter example.
example.expected_result: Prints PLLDN, usually with a filename and line-number prefix from trace.

licenses.scope: The Haxe compiler itself, as described by the Haxe Foundation licensing page.
licenses.notice: Compiler redistribution obligations are separate from the licensing of your own Haxe source and generated output.

licenses.scope: The Haxe standard library grant; additional target libraries and runtimes have their own terms.
licenses.notice: Retain required notices when distributing covered library material and inspect target dependencies separately.

implementation.name: Hy compiler on Python
implementation.version_scope: Hy 1.3.1 manual, Python AST compilation and hy filename.hy workflow; Python compatibility follows the selected Hy release.

Hy 1.3.1 tutorial: forms, print and macros
Hy 1.3.1 command-line interface
Hy 1.3.1: language scope and Python interoperability

fit.text: Lisp-style forms and macros within Python's ecosystem. Python built-ins and third-party libraries remain available through Hy's Python interoperability.

prerequisites.text: Use a Python version supported by the installed Hy release and install Hy in that environment. Learn prefix forms and Python's object and library model.

execution.text: Hy transforms source into Python AST objects and runs on Python; hy hello.hy executes a file and hy starts a REPL.

behavior.text: Calls use parenthesized prefix forms. Macros transform code at compile time, while ordinary function calls run with Python's semantics.

tooling.text: Use the hy REPL, hy2py to inspect a Python representation, and hyc for bytecode compilation. These serve different workflows.

maintenance.text: Check Hy and Python compatibility together. A Python library's requirements still apply when it is called through Hy.

costs.text: Include the Python environment and third-party dependencies in deployment planning. Hy's MIT grant does not establish those dependencies' licenses.

example.run_instructions: With Hy installed in a compatible Python environment, save hello.hy and run hy hello.hy. The print call uses Python's built-in function.
example.expected_result: Prints PLLDN followed by a newline.

licenses.scope: Hy source covered by the repository's MIT license; the Python interpreter and imported packages are separate components.
licenses.notice: Preserve the MIT notice for covered redistributed material and inspect the selected Python distribution and dependencies separately.
